source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying count-based exploration and intrinsic motivation (pseudo-count)
finding: Derives a pseudo-count from any density model (CTS on pixels). Bonus is proportional to N^(-1/2), like MBIE-EB. Pseudo-count is near zero for a novel event and grows about linearly with repeats.
numbers: Montezuma's Revenge: policy passes through 15 of 24 rooms within 50M frames; one run reaches about 6600 points by 100M frames (half of DQN's 200M). Games shown: Montezuma, Freeway, Venture, H.E.R.O., Private Eye.
quote: Pseudo-counts are roughly zero for novel events
limits: Only the best run reaches 6600; bonus needs tuning per game.
agent_relevance: S3 history of directions tried: a count that generalises (similar items share counts) fits a history of tried directions better than exact-match counts.

source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying count-based exploration and intrinsic motivation (theory)
finding: Theorem 1: a bonus proportional to N^(-1/2) is at least as exploratory as an information-gain bonus. Theorem 2: pseudo-count over empirical count tends to a limit for models consistent in the tabular case. Cites Kolter and Ng (2009): bonuses not of count form cannot be PAC-MDP.
numbers: No empirical numbers; theorems.
limits: Deep density models only approximately meet the assumptions.
agent_relevance: Count form gives a principled decay: each retry of a similar direction should shrink its bonus by 1/sqrt(n).

source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying count-based exploration and intrinsic motivation (A3C+ on 60 games)
finding: Added the pseudo-count bonus to A3C and trained on 60 Atari games with and without it.
numbers: A3C fails (not 50% above random) in 15 games; A3C+ fails in 10, of which 8 are games where DQN also fails. Slightly better median; clearly better on at least a quarter of games.
limits: Authors note epsilon-greedy suffices for most Atari games, so gains are concentrated in a minority.
agent_relevance: A bonus helps on a minority of problems. Do not switch exploration on by default; gate it at an impasse.

source: Tang et al. (2017) #Exploration: a study of count-based exploration with hashing
finding: Map states to hash codes (SimHash, or a learned autoencoder code) and count buckets; bonus beta/sqrt(n). Even raw-pixel SimHash helps. Granularity and keeping relevant information in the hash decide success.
numbers: Table 1 (50M steps, TRPO): Freeway baseline 16.5 vs pixel-SimHash 31.6; Frostbite 2869 vs 4683; Venture 121 vs 616 (Double-DQN 1172). Montezuma: baseline 0, pixel-SimHash 238 in the table row; AE-SimHash 0 in one row, BASS-SimHash larger.
quote: Surprisingly, TRPO-pixel-SimHash already outperforms the baseline
limits: PDF table text is partly interleaved, so Montezuma row values are approximate; Montezuma depends on preprocessing.
agent_relevance: Counting needs a good state abstraction. For the agent, define 'same direction' by a hash of the key idea, not exact text.

source: Ostrovski et al. (2017) Count-based exploration with neural density models (DQN-PixelCNN)
finding: PixelCNN gives pseudo-counts for DQN and Reactor. Surprising finding: the mixed Monte Carlo return update, not only the bonus, is a strong facilitator of exploration in sparse games.
numbers: Reactor-PixelCNN beats Reactor in about 50 games (best score in 52 by maximum, 51 by AUC). Record peaks in run: 900 Gravitar, 6,600 Montezuma, 39,000 Private Eye, 1,500 Venture.
quote: the mixed Monte Carlo update is a powerful facilitator of exploration
limits: Peaks are best runs; MMC explains most of the progress in some games; PG decay schedule and learning rate are sensitive.
agent_relevance: Credit assignment matters as much as the bonus: a bonus for untried directions pays only if outcomes propagate back to the choice.

source: Ostrovski et al. (2017) intrinsic reward behaviour
finding: Intrinsic reward in Montezuma spikes on large state changes such as switching rooms. The model is non-stationary, so prediction gain decay must be adapted.
numbers: Fig. 10 (qualitative): bonus peaks at room transitions; Fig. 9 shows PG on log scale decaying over training.
limits: Qualitative figure.
agent_relevance: Density-model quality sets what counts as new. An LLM embedding could serve as density source for text states.

source: Machado, Bellemare, Bowling (2018) Count-based exploration with the successor representation
finding: The norm of the successor representation acts as an implicit visit count; the substochastic SR counts state visits. Sarsa+SR matches theoretically efficient tabular methods and is state of the art in low-sample Atari.
numbers: Atari 2600 low-sample regime (abstract claim); no density model needed.
limits: Low-sample regime only, not the 200M-frame comparison.
agent_relevance: Counts can come from structure (transition similarity) without a pixel density model.

source: Pathak et al. (2017) Curiosity-driven exploration by self-supervised prediction (ICM)
finding: Reward = forward-model prediction error in a feature space trained with an inverse model, so uncontrollable parts are ignored. Tested in VizDoom and Super Mario Bros (Mario trained with curiosity only).
numbers: In sparse VizDoom, ICM+A3C solves tasks where epsilon-greedy A3C fails as goal distance grows; ICM-pixels (no inverse model) does worse. A noisy TV added to a Unity maze degrades results.
limits: Noisy-TV problem acknowledged; precise percentages not extracted.
agent_relevance: Prediction-error novelty can be hijacked by noise. In an LLM loop, rewarding 'surprising output' invites rambling.

source: Burda et al. (2018) Large-scale study of curiosity-driven learning
finding: First large study of pure curiosity (no extrinsic reward) across 54 environments including Atari. Random features suffice for many benchmarks; learned features generalise better (new Mario levels). Prediction rewards fail with stochastic transitions.
numbers: 54 benchmark environments; intrinsic curiosity aligns with hand-designed score in many.
limits: Alignment with score partly reflects game design; noisy-TV limit.
agent_relevance: Pure novelty looks productive only when the benchmark rewards exploring.

source: Burda et al. (2018) Exploration by random network distillation (RND)
finding: Bonus = error predicting a fixed random network's output; avoids stochastic-transition and model-misspecification traps. Two value heads allow non-episodic intrinsic return with episodic extrinsic return.
numbers: Pure exploration (no extrinsic reward) finds more than half of the 24 rooms in Montezuma. Best agent often finds 22 of 24 and occasionally passes level 1. Best published on Venture and Gravitar at the time.
limits: Much of the gain is engineering (non-episodic streams, many parallel environments); Taiga et al. did not reproduce with the plain bonus.
agent_relevance: Keep novelty credit across episodes (lifelong), but judge the final answer on separate episodic criteria.

source: Burda et al. (2018) RND ablations
finding: Non-episodic intrinsic stream increases rooms found compared with episodic; effect on mean return is smaller because extrinsic reward preserves useful behaviour. Spikes in the bonus correspond to meaningful events.
numbers: Pure-exploration best run explored 21 rooms for the lower-discount setting; more parallel environments raise mean return.
limits: Ablations are on one game.
agent_relevance: Lifelong memory of tried directions across sub-problems beats resetting at each one.

source: Taiga et al. (2019) On bonus-based exploration methods in the ALE (benchmark)
finding: Same Rainbow agent, 200M frames, 5 seeds, hyperparameters tuned only on Montezuma. Pseudo-count CTS, RND, ICM, NoisyNets, epsilon-greedy compared. Newer bonuses did not beat the 2016 pseudo-count.
numbers: Montezuma: epsilon-greedy poor; others consistently reach 2500; CTS pseudo-count reaches 5000 within 200M frames. On easy games the pseudo-count is worse on every game except Seaquest; RND and ICM only match epsilon-greedy; NoisyNets most consistent.
limits: Their RND uses only the bonus, without the paper's extra techniques; hard-game generalisation limited.
agent_relevance: Bonus-based methods are generally detrimental in the context of easy exploration problems

source: Taiga et al. (2019) boundary condition
finding: Exploration bonuses skew the reward landscape. Benefit seen on a few games becomes a loss when exploration is not the bottleneck.
numbers: Reversed trend on Asterix, Seaquest and the Atari training set versus Montezuma.
limits: Atari only.
agent_relevance: Strong boundary condition: gate novelty seeking on an impasse signal; anneal it when answers are converging.

source: Ecoffet et al. (2019) Go-Explore
finding: Archive of visited cells; return to a promising cell, then explore from it. Counts of cell visits select which cell to return to. Avoids detachment and derailment seen in bonus agents.
numbers: Montezuma: over 43,000 points with no domain knowledge (almost 4x prior state of the art); mean over 650,000 with domain knowledge; max 18 million. Pitfall: first algorithm above zero (with domain knowledge).
quote: almost 4 times the previous state of the art
limits: Relies on resettable states or determinism in phase one; domain variant uses hand cell features.
agent_relevance: Maps to S3: keep an archive of tried directions and return to one explicitly instead of hoping a bonus pulls back.

source: Badia et al. (2020) Never Give Up
finding: Episodic novelty (kNN over embeddings of controllable states in an episodic memory) multiplied by a lifelong RND modulator; learns a family of policies with different exploration weights.
numbers: Median human-normalised score 1344.0% on the remaining games; mean 8,400 on Pitfall! without demonstrations.
limits: About 35 billion frames of training; heavy compute.
agent_relevance: Two-timescale novelty: within this problem (episodic) and across problems (lifelong) is a ready design for S3.

source: Badia et al. (2020) Agent57
finding: First deep RL agent above the human baseline on all 57 Atari games, adding an adaptive bandit that picks the exploration weight and a split value function.
numbers: MuZero and R2D2 had exceeded 100% human-normalised on 51 and 52 games; Agent57 exceeds on all 57 with one hyperparameter set.
limits: Gain comes from many parts, not counting alone.
agent_relevance: A meta-controller choosing the explore weight per run links to operator selection by bandits (subfield 01).

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2 as bandit agents over 32 prompt designs. Only GPT-4 with chain-of-thought and an externally summarised history (sufficient statistics) explored satisfactorily.
numbers: Basic GPT-4 prompt: suffix failure (best arm never chosen after early rounds) in over 60% of replicates. Only three GPT-4 configurations avoided suffix failures. Horizon T=100, Bernoulli bandits.
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Small bandits; summarising may be impossible in complex tasks.
agent_relevance: Do the counting outside the model: give the LLM a table of per-direction counts, not raw history.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) failure mode
finding: Models behave like greedy: lock onto an early apparent best arm and stop sampling others. Chain-of-thought on raw history did not fix it; UCB and Thompson sampling baselines do not show it.
numbers: Suffix failure frequency plotted for all configurations at T=100.
limits: Prompt framing, temperature and model interact.
agent_relevance: Without an external count, S3 will collapse onto the first plausible direction (premature exploitation).

source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding pretraining in RL with LLMs (ELLM)
finding: Argues count and prediction novelty reward endless meaningless novelty. ELLM asks an LLM for plausible common-sense goals given the state and rewards achieving them (Crafter, Housekeep).
numbers: Abstract: ELLM-trained agents cover more common-sense behaviours in pretraining and match or improve downstream; figures not extracted.
limits: Depends on text description of state and LLM quality.
agent_relevance: Counts alone reward trivial novelty; combine a count with an LLM judge of whether a direction is meaningful.

source: Zhang, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2024) OMNI
finding: Foundation model as a model of interestingness picks tasks that are learnable and interesting; beats uniform sampling and learning-progress-only baselines.
numbers: Abstract-level claim read; margins not extracted.
limits: Interestingness inherits FM biases toward human-style tasks.
agent_relevance: Replace exact-match counts by an LLM judgement of semantic novelty: define 'same' semantically.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager
finding: LLM agent with an automatic curriculum proposing the next task to maximise discovery given its history; described by authors as in-context novelty search.
numbers: Random curriculum cuts discovered item count by 93%; removing self-verification cuts it by 73%.
limits: Minecraft-specific; leans on GPT-4 game knowledge.
agent_relevance: An existing LLM agent loop doing exploration with a history list and no numeric counts; the history is its S3.

source: Cheng et al. (2025) Reasoning with exploration: an entropy perspective
finding: High-entropy tokens correlate with pivotal tokens, reflective actions and rare behaviours. Adds an entropy term to the advantage (one line of code) to favour longer reasoning chains.
numbers: Gains on Pass@K at large K and Pass@1 on AIME 2024/2025 and AMC; exact deltas not extracted.
limits: Token entropy is a proxy for novelty, not a state count; training-time.
agent_relevance: LLM-RL analogue of a count bonus; needs training, so outside our scaffold-only scope.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Self-exploring language models (SELM)
finding: Adds an optimism term (max over response reward) to preference optimisation so the LLM explores novel favourable responses; DPO instead passively favours unseen extrapolations.
numbers: Beats iterative DPO with Zephyr-7B-SFT on instruction benchmarks; numbers not extracted.
limits: Training-time method.
agent_relevance: Optimism under uncertainty, the principle behind count bonuses, applied at response level.

source: Strehl and Littman (2008) MBIE-EB
finding: Count bonus beta/sqrt(N(s,a)) added to the Bellman backup gives PAC-MDP efficiency in tabular MDPs. Seen only as cited in Bellemare 2016.
limits: Tabular only; not opened.
agent_relevance: Source of the 1/sqrt(n) form.

source: Kolter and Ng (2009) Near-Bayesian exploration in polynomial time
finding: Shows bonuses not proportional to 1/N cannot be PAC-MDP; used by Bellemare 2016 against prediction-gain bonuses. Seen only via citation.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Theory support for count-shaped decay.
